title: Introduction & Scientific Method
text:
Overview
The scientific method is a step-by-step process for exploring how the world works: observation → question → hypothesis → experiment → data collection → data analysis → conclusion. It isn’t a straight line — scientists loop back and revise as they learn more.

title: Introduction & Scientific Method
text:
Key Vocabulary


hypothesis — a testable, falsifiable proposed explanation
falsifiable — capable of being proven wrong by evidence
independent variable — the factor the experimenter deliberately changes
dependent variable — the factor that is measured
control group — the baseline group that does not receive the treatment, used for comparison
confounding variable — an outside factor that could distort the result
precision — how closely repeated measurements agree with each other
accuracy — how close a measurement is to the true value

title: Introduction & Scientific Method
text:
Precision vs. Accuracy
It’s easy to confuse these two. A measurement can be precise but not accurate (consistent, but consistently wrong due to a systematic error), or accurate but not precise (right on average, but scattered).

title: Introduction & Scientific Method
text:
Case Study: Penicillin
Alexander Fleming’s 1928 discovery of penicillin is a real example of the full scientific method in action — from an accidental observation (mould killing bacteria on a forgotten petri dish) to a hypothesis, experiments, and a conclusion that changed medicine. See the slides for the full walkthrough.

title: Welcome to Scientific English
text:
Welcome!

A science course, taught in English
Real biology, and the English that scientists use to talk about it
Today: the course, your teacher, and you


Plan about 20-25 minutes for this session, then move on to How to Study. Speak slowly and clearly, and use gestures and the board: for many students this is the first lesson fully in English. Reassure them that they are not expected to understand every word.

title: Welcome to Scientific English
text:
Who Am I?




Marco Chiapello
I studied biology at the University of Turin, and have a PhD in Fungal Biology and Biotechnology.
I worked in research and teaching in Italy, the UK, and the Switzerland.
Currently I work at Agilent Technologies, a life sciences, diagnostics, and analytical laboratory technology company. It helps scientists and laboratories measure, analyze, diagnose, and understand chemical and biological samples.















Keep it short and personal: a photo of your lab, your field work, or an object from your work makes it concrete. Students are curious about what a scientist actually does all day.

title: Welcome to Scientific English
text:
Guess the Fact
Two of these are true, one is false. Which one is the lie?

My English grade in high school was 4/10.
I am currently working only in English.
I am working in a biology laboratory.


Students vote with their hands (1, 2 or 3) before you reveal the answer. Ask a few students to explain their choice in English: “I think number 2 is false, because…”. This models the game they will play next.

title: Welcome to Scientific English
text:
Now It’s Your Turn

Move from the teacher to the students. The goal is that everyone says at least one sentence in English today.

title: Welcome to Scientific English
text:
Introduce Yourself
Say these three things:

My name is …
One thing I like is …
One word that describes me is …
What I want to be when I grow up is …


Go around the room quickly, about 20 seconds per student. Write the sentence frames on the board. If the class is large, do it in groups of four and then ask one student per group to introduce someone else (“This is Marco, he likes…”).

title: Welcome to Scientific English
text:
Find Someone Who …



has been to an English-speaking country



wants to study medicine or biology



has watched a science documentary this month



can name a famous scientist (not Einstein!)



knows what DNA stands for





Give 5 minutes. Rule: they can only ask in English (“Have you ever…?”, “Do you want to…?”). At the end, ask who completed the most rows and check a few answers with the class. The DNA question is a nice bridge to the course content: deoxyribonucleic acid.

title: How to Study
text:
How to Study

Study strategies backed by cognitive science
Some habits feel productive but do not produce lasting learning
Today: prepare your body and mind, avoid what does not work, learn six strategies that do


Open by asking how they currently study: highlighting, re-reading notes, cramming the night before? Ask who has used flashcards. Do not judge the answers. The goal is to find out what actually works, not what feels productive.

title: How to Study
text:
Goals of the Project

Improve learning for students
Understand how we learn
Improve education and science
Propose strategies based on scientific evidence


These materials come from the Learning Scientists, a group of cognitive psychologists (Yana Weinstein and Megan Smith, with illustrator Oliver Caviglioli), funded by the APS Fund for Teaching and Public Understanding of Psychological Science. Point out the source so students see this is research, not opinion. Full references are on the session material page.

title: How to Study
section: Your Brain Is Part of Your Body
text:
Your Brain Is Part of Your Body






This sets up the next two slides: learning is a physical process. Sleep, exercise and food affect memory and attention, so preparing your body is part of studying. Ask: when did you last study well after a bad night of sleep?

title: How to Study
text:
Preparing Your Body and Mind (1/2)



Keep a sleep schedule: the more regular it is, the easier it is to fall asleep and wake up
Build a wind-down routine so your body learns that it is time to rest
Put your phone away before bed: interacting with it keeps your mind active when it should be winding down





Ask students to estimate how many hours they sleep and when they put the phone away. Keep it non-judgmental. Connect to memory: memories are consolidated during sleep, so an all-nighter before an exam weakens recall the next day.

title: How to Study
text:
Preparing Your Body and Mind (2/2)



Exercise regularly: good for physical and mental health
Stay hydrated: dehydration hurts your ability to think and remember
Eat healthy snacks: fruit and vegetables while you study, because thinking is hard work





Quick poll: how many of you drank water during the last lesson? Make the point that studying is physically demanding, so it is worth looking after yourself. Do not go beyond the claims on the slide.

title: How to Study
text:
The Myth of Multitasking

This is the most important correction in the session. Name the myth and ask what students think it means before showing the next slide.

title: How to Study
text:
What Is Multitasking?



The term is misleading
We do not do several tasks at once: we switch between them
A few minutes of study, then TV, then texting, then back to study
Our attention can only be on one task at any given time





Ask: when you say you are studying while listening to music, what happens when a notification arrives? Each switch costs time and attention, so the study time is split and less is learned. Ask students to name their own switching habits.

title: How to Study
text:
Focusing Your Learning (1/2)



Stick to a routine: it puts you in a studying state of mind. Choose something you find pleasant and relaxing
Try the Pomodoro technique: focused work in short blocks of about 25 minutes, with a short break in between





Pomodoro means “tomato” in Italian: the original timer was a tomato-shaped kitchen timer. Ask students to try one 25-minute block this week and report back at the next session.

title: How to Study
text:
Focusing Your Learning (2/2)

Use apps to reduce distractions on your phone and computer (for example Cold Turkey or Forest)
Create accountability groups with peers: studying in pairs or groups makes it easier to stay on task


Cold Turkey blocks distracting websites; Forest grows a virtual tree while you stay off your phone. For accountability: everyone works on their own assignment, but in the same room, so you are less tempted to drift.

title: How to Study
text:
Avoid Strategies That Don’t Work

Students often rely on methods that feel productive but produce weak long-term learning. The next slides show which ones, and how to make them more effective.

title: How to Study
section: Popular Strategies: How to Make Them Work (1/2)
text:
Popular Strategies: How to Make Them Work (1/2)



Re-reading builds confidence but not much learning. Combine it with spaced and retrieval practice
Flashcards are powerful when you use them to recall from memory, not just to read. Keep testing yourself even after a correct answer





Re-reading feels fluent, so students mistake fluency for learning. Demonstrate the difference: read a paragraph, close the book and write what you remember, then compare. The gap is where the learning happens.

title: How to Study
section: Popular Strategies: How to Make Them Work (2/2)
text:
Popular Strategies: How to Make Them Work (2/2)

Note-taking: complete notes that capture the main concepts, summarised in your own words (the Cornell method)
Outlining: read the material twice. The first time, do nothing else. The second time, record the main points


The Cornell method: a notes column, a cue column with questions, and a summary at the bottom. The outlining trick separates understanding from extracting. The next few slides show how to set up Cornell notes. Connect back to the six strategies: these are variants of retrieval practice and elaboration.

title: How to Study
text:
Cornell Note-Taking
A simple page layout that turns your notes into a study tool

Introduce the Cornell method as the concrete version of the note-taking tip from the previous slide. It was developed at Cornell University in the 1950s. The goal of this short section is that students can set up a Cornell page in their notebook this week.

title: How to Study
text:
Cornell Notes: The Page Layout




Cue columnkeywords and questions


Notes columnmain ideas, facts, examples, drawings


Summary: the whole page in 2-3 sentences, in your own words






A Cornell page, filled in




Draw this on the board or show a real notebook page. Left column about one third of the width, notes on the right, summary in a strip at the bottom. Leave the cue column and summary empty during the lesson: they are filled in afterwards.

title: How to Study
text:
Cornell Notes: Five Steps

Record: take notes in the right column during the lesson, in your own words
Question: after class, write questions and keywords in the cue column
Recite: cover the notes column and answer each cue from memory
Summarize: write the main idea of the page in the bottom box
Review: come back to the page after a few days and again after a few weeks


Steps 1 and 4 are note-taking and elaboration. Step 3 is retrieval practice and step 5 is spaced practice, so the Cornell method already combines several of the six strategies we are about to see. Ask students which step they think is the most useful, and which they are most likely to skip (usually step 3).

title: How to Study
text:
Cornell Notes: Example







Cue column
Notes column




What is a hypothesis?
A testable, falsifiable explanation for an observation


Why a control group?
Baseline for comparison, shows the effect of the treatment


Precision vs. accuracy?
Precision: repeated results agree. Accuracy: close to the true value



Summary: A good experiment changes one variable and compares it with a control.

Use content from the next lesson so students see it is practical. Stress that the cues are real questions that you could answer out loud, not single words.

title: How to Study
text:
Cornell Notes: Hold On!

Do not copy the teacher or the book word for word: rewrite in your own words
Write cues that are questions, not just titles
Do not skip step 3: reading the notes again is not retrieval, covering them and answering is
Fill in the cue column and summary the same day, while you still remember the lesson


Link to the “Hold on” warnings of retrieval practice and elaboration that come later. Homework suggestion: use the Cornell layout for the notes of the next lesson.

title: How to Study
text:
Cornell Notes: A Full Example



Cornell notes on this lesson: How to Study



This page shows what a student’s Cornell notes on today’s lesson could look like. Point out the three zones: the questions on the left are written after class, the notes on the right during class, and the summary at the bottom last. Challenge: cover the right column and answer each question from memory.

title: How to Study
text:
Six Strategies for Effective Learning



Learning Scientists: Six Strategies for Effective Learning



This is the overview of the six strategies we will study: retrieval practice, spaced practice, dual coding, interleaving, concrete examples and elaboration. Each strategy has a “How to do it” part and “Hold on” warnings. The highlighted hexagon in each section shows which strategy you are looking at.

title: How to Study
text:
Retrieval Practice






Retrieval practice means bringing information to mind, not just looking at it. It is the strategy with the strongest support in the research, so give it time in the session.

title: How to Study
text:
Retrieval Practice: Video


The Learning Scientists, “Retrieval Practice: A video for Students”. Play it in class, then ask students to name one way they could use the strategy this week.

title: How to Study
text:
Retrieval Practice: Write or Sketch






Put away your class materials, write or sketch everything you know, then check the materials for what you missed.

title: How to Study
text:
Retrieval Practice: Trade Tests






Take as many practice tests as you can. If there are none, make your own and trade with a friend.

title: How to Study
text:
Retrieval Practice: Flashcards






Flashcards work when you practise recalling the answer, and go beyond definitions to links between ideas. Ask students to try a three-minute blank-page recall of today’s lesson now, then compare with the slides.

title: How to Study
section: Retrieval Practice: Hold On! (check your materials)
text:
Retrieval Practice: Hold On! (check your materials)






Retrieval works best when you check your materials afterwards.

title: How to Study
section: Retrieval Practice: Hold On! (retrieval is hard)
text:
Retrieval Practice: Hold On! (retrieval is hard)






Retrieval is supposed to feel hard. Stress that struggling is evidence the strategy is working.

title: How to Study
section: Retrieval Practice: Hold On! (more than definitions)
text:
Retrieval Practice: Hold On! (more than definitions)






Warn against recalling only definitions: students should also recall main ideas, relationships and new examples.

title: How to Study
text:
Spaced Practice






Spaced practice means spreading study over time instead of cramming. Start with the slide’s example: five hours spread over two weeks works better than five hours in one go.

title: How to Study
text:
Spaced Practice: Video


The Learning Scientists, “Study Strategies: Spaced Practice”. Play it in class, then ask students to name one way they could use the strategy this week.

title: How to Study
text:
Spaced Practice: Plan Early






Start planning early for exams and set aside a little time every day. Ask students how they could spread their revision this week.

title: How to Study
section: Spaced Practice: Review After a Delay
text:
Spaced Practice: Review After a Delay






Review each lesson after a delay, not right after class.

title: How to Study
text:
Spaced Practice: Revisit Older Material






After reviewing the most recent class, go back to important older material from a week or a month ago. Ask students when they last reviewed the lesson from the previous session.

title: How to Study
section: Spaced Practice: Hold On! (sit down with strategies)
text:
Spaced Practice: Hold On! (sit down with strategies)






When you sit down to study, use effective strategies rather than just re-reading your notes.

title: How to Study
section: Spaced Practice: Hold On! (forgetting is useful)
text:
Spaced Practice: Hold On! (forgetting is useful)






Feeling that you forget things from day to day is normal and useful: having to retrieve the memory is what strengthens it.

title: How to Study
section: Spaced Practice: Hold On! (small spaces add up)
text:
Spaced Practice: Hold On! (small spaces add up)






Small spaced sessions of a few days each add up to much more than one long session.

title: How to Study
text:
Dual Coding






Dual coding means combining words and visuals. Using both gives you two ways to retrieve the same idea.

title: How to Study
text:
Dual Coding: Video


The Learning Scientists, “Dual Coding: A Video For Students”. Play it in class, then ask students to name one way they could use the strategy this week.

title: How to Study
text:
Dual Coding: Find the Visuals






Look at your class materials and find the visuals. Compare them with the words.

title: How to Study
text:
Dual Coding: Explain the Visual






Look at a visual and explain in your own words what it means.

title: How to Study
text:
Dual Coding: Draw Your Own






Take information you are trying to learn and draw visuals to go along with it.

title: How to Study
text:
Dual Coding: Hold On! (many formats)






Try different ways to represent the information visually: an infographic, a timeline, a cartoon strip, a diagram or a graphic organizer. You can skip the next examples if you are short on time.

title: How to Study
text:
Dual Coding: Infographic






An infographic combines a few numbers, short labels and simple shapes.

title: How to Study
text:
Dual Coding: Timeline






A timeline is useful for history: events in order, with dates.

title: How to Study
text:
Dual Coding: Cartoon Strip






A cartoon strip works well for a sequence of steps, such as a process.

title: How to Study
text:
Dual Coding: Diagram






A diagram shows parts that work together, for example the organs of the body in biology.

title: How to Study
text:
Dual Coding: Graphic Organizer






A graphic organizer shows how ideas are linked. Ask which format suits each subject best.

title: How to Study
section: Dual Coding: Hold On! (draw from memory)
text:
Dual Coding: Hold On! (draw from memory)






Work up to drawing from memory. Start with the class material open, then close it and draw what you remember.

title: How to Study
text:
Interleaving






Interleaving means switching between different topics during a study session, instead of studying one topic until it is finished.

title: How to Study
text:
Interleaving: Video


The Learning Scientists, “Interleaving: A Video for Students”. Play it in class, then ask students to name one way they could use the strategy this week.

title: How to Study
text:
Interleaving: Switch Between Topics






Study topic A, then B, then C. Do not study one idea for too long.

title: How to Study
text:
Interleaving: Mix the Order






Go back over the ideas in different orders in later study sessions to strengthen understanding.

title: How to Study
text:
Interleaving: Link the Ideas






Make links between different ideas as you switch between them.

title: How to Study
section: Interleaving: Hold On! (do not switch too often)
text:
Interleaving: Hold On! (do not switch too often)






Switching is good, but not so often that you spend too little time on any one idea. You need to understand each one.

title: How to Study
text:
Interleaving: Hold On! (it feels harder)






Interleaving will feel harder than blocking, and that is the point. Ask students to suggest how they could interleave their revision for two subjects this week.

title: How to Study
text:
Concrete Examples






Concrete examples means using specific cases to understand abstract ideas. Ask students for a concrete example of a concept from this course.

title: How to Study
text:
Concrete Examples: Video


The Learning Scientists, “Concrete Examples: A Video for Students”. Play it in class, then ask students to name one way they could use the strategy this week.

title: How to Study
text:
Concrete Examples: Collect Them






Collect the examples your teacher uses, and look in your class materials for more.

title: How to Study
text:
Concrete Examples: Link Each One






Make the link between the idea and each example, so you understand how the example applies.

title: How to Study
text:
Concrete Examples: Share Them






Share examples with friends and explain them to each other.

title: How to Study
text:
Concrete Examples: Hold On! (check examples)






Not every example you find online is used correctly. Check examples with the teacher.

title: How to Study
section: Concrete Examples: Hold On! (make your own)
text:
Concrete Examples: Hold On! (make your own)






The strongest examples are the ones you create yourself.

title: How to Study
text:
Elaboration






Elaboration means explaining and describing ideas with many details. Ask a question about why something works, then find the answer and explain it to a classmate.

title: How to Study
text:
Elaboration: Video


The Learning Scientists, “Elaboration: A Video for Students”. Play it in class, then ask students to name one way they could use the strategy this week.

title: How to Study
text:
Elaboration: Ask Why and How






Ask yourself “how” and “why” questions while studying, then find the answers in the class materials and discuss them with classmates.

title: How to Study
text:
Elaboration: Connect Ideas






Take two ideas and ask how they are similar and different. This forces you to explain how they work together.

title: How to Study
text:
Elaboration: Use Your Own Experience






Link new ideas to your own experiences. Ask for a personal example from the class.

title: How to Study
text:
Elaboration: Hold On! (accuracy)






Elaborations must be accurate, so check them against the class materials or ask the teacher.

title: How to Study
text:
Elaboration: Hold On! (explain without notes)






You should be able to explain without looking at your notes. That is what turns elaboration into retrieval practice.

title: How to Study
text:
Bonus: NotebookLM
A Google AI tool that is a great study partner

Introduce the last tool of the session. The question to ask students: is this AI helping me learn, or doing the learning for me? Everything in this section is about the first.

title: How to Study
text:
What Is NotebookLM?



Made by Google, free with a Google account
You upload your own sources: class slides, PDFs, notes, web pages
Answers come from your documents, with citations you can check





Check the current features and any school restrictions before the lesson at notebooklm.google.com, since Google updates the tool often. For students under 18, confirm the school’s policy on Google accounts and AI tools. Show the interface live if possible.

title: How to Study
section: Two Ways to Use an AI
text:
Two Ways to Use an AI



AI writes for you
AI helps you learn




“Write my essay on DNA”
“Quiz me on DNA, one question at a time”


You copy, and learn nothing
You answer, and the AI checks


The thinking happens in the AI
The thinking happens in your head


Weak retention
Retrieval practice, elaboration, spacing




Ask: which of these two columns is the homework? The left column produces a text you do not understand. The right column produces understanding you can use in the exam. The AI should be the study partner, not the author.

title: How to Study
text:
NotebookLM for Learning: Four Prompts

“Quiz me on this chapter, one question at a time. Wait for my answer before you continue.”
“I will explain photosynthesis in my own words. Point out what I missed, using only my sources.”
“Make flashcards from my notes. I will recall first, then check.”
“Give me a concept map with blanks, and ask me to fill in the links.”


Each prompt turns the tool into retrieval practice or elaboration. Model one prompt live with a passage from the class materials, then ask a student to try another. Stress: “using only my sources” keeps the answers accurate.

title: How to Study
text:
NotebookLM: Rules of Use

Your brain does the work: answer before you look at the AI’s answer
Check against the sources: citations let you verify every claim
Never hand in AI text as your own writing: use it to understand, then write yourself


Connect back to the myth of multitasking and to retrieval practice: the best prompt is one that makes you recall, not one that gives you the answer. Ask students for an example of a prompt they would use this week.

title: How to Study
text:
Recap

Prepare your body and mind: sleep, exercise, water, healthy snacks
Multitasking is switching; attention can only be on one thing at a time
Re-reading and cramming feel productive but work poorly
Six strategies: retrieval practice, spaced practice, dual coding, interleaving, concrete examples, elaboration
NotebookLM can be a study partner, as long as you do the thinking

Session 2 Worksheet: Let’s Correct It





Take out your worksheet Exploring the Scientific Method and a pen of a different colour.

True or False (1–5)
Matching (6–13)
Identifying variables and groups (14–25)

title: Understanding DNA
text:
Worksheet — True or False

If false, the underlined word is replaced to make the sentence correct.








#
Statement
Answer




1
Forming a hypothesis is the first step of the scientific method.
False → making an observation


2
A scientific law is different from a theory because it describes something in nature without attempting to explain it.
True


3
For a hypothesis to be testable, scientists must be able to carry out investigations that will either support or disprove it.
True


4
The experimental group is the group that is left alone during the experiment.
False → control group


5
The manipulated variable is the same thing as the independent variable.
True





1: science starts with an observation, then a question; the hypothesis comes third. 2: a law DESCRIBES what happens (e.g. the law of gravity: objects fall); a theory EXPLAINS why. A theory never “grows up” into a law: they do different jobs. 3: this is falsifiability from Session 2. 4: the control group is left alone, so it gives the baseline. 5: manipulated = independent = the one we change; responding = dependent = the one we measure.

19. redness of the skin
20. arm with the new formula
21. arm with the leading formula


Sunlight: 12 plants get normal sunlight, half of them also stay under bright lamps all night; height after 6 weeks
22. amount of light
23. plant height (growth)
24. plants kept under the lamps
25. plants with just normal sun





Reveal row by row (4 clicks per scenario). Sunscreen is the interesting one: the control is NOT “no sunscreen” but the leading formula, because the question is whether the new one is BETTER than what already exists. Each person is their own control (one arm each), which removes differences between people’s skin: a smart design. Ask: what variables must be kept the same in the plant experiment? (water, soil, pot size, type of plant, temperature.)

title: Understanding DNA
text:
DNA: The Molecule of Life


The instruction manual for every living thing, from bacteria to humans
Found in almost every cell of your body
Copied and passed on from parents to children


Start with a question: “What do you already know about DNA?” Collect a few words on the board (genes, double helix, inheritance, crime scenes…). Then: DNA is not alive and does not “do” anything by itself. It is information, like a recipe book. The cell reads it to build and run the organism.

title: Understanding DNA
text:
What Does “DNA” Stand For?











Scientific English tip: long scientific words are often built from smaller parts. If you know the parts, you can decode the word. “De-oxy” = without oxygen (the sugar deoxyribose has one oxygen atom less than ribose, the sugar in RNA). “Nucleic” because Friedrich Miescher first isolated it from cell nuclei in 1869 (he called it “nuclein”). “Acid” because of the phosphate groups. The structures: both sugars have a ring of 4 carbons and 1 oxygen; carbons are numbered 1′ to 5′ (“one prime” to “five prime”). The only difference is carbon 2′: OH in ribose, just H in deoxyribose. Students do not need to memorise the structures, only the idea “deoxy = one oxygen missing”. (The 5′ and 1′ carbons are where the phosphate and the base attach in a nucleotide: next slide.) Ask: what could “ribonucleic acid” (RNA) mean?

title: Understanding DNA
text:
The Building Block: the Nucleotide

DNA is a polymer: a long chain of millions of nucleotides.

Vocabulary: polymer — a large molecule made of many repeated units (poly = many, mer = part).


Every nucleotide has the same phosphate and the same sugar. Only the base changes, and there are only four kinds. So all the information in DNA is in the ORDER of the bases, the way all the information in a book is in the order of the letters.

title: Understanding DNA
text:
Four Bases, Two Families


Purines (A, G) are bigger: two rings. Pyrimidines (C, T) are smaller: one ring. In RNA, thymine is replaced by uracil (U), another pyrimidine. Mnemonics: “Pure As Gold” for purines; “CUT the Py” for pyrimidines. Students do not need to learn the chemical structures, only the two families and which base belongs to which.

title: Understanding DNA
text:
The Base-Pairing Rule

A always pairs with T, G always pairs with C. The two strands are complementary.

A purine always pairs with a pyrimidine, so every rung of the ladder has the same width and the helix is regular. Hydrogen bonds are weak, so the two strands can be separated (“unzipped”) without breaking the strands themselves. That will matter for replication. G–C pairs have three bonds, so DNA rich in G and C is harder to separate (it melts at a higher temperature).

title: Understanding DNA
text:
Complementary Strands — Try It
If one strand reads:

A T G C C T A G G A

What does the other strand read?


T A C G G A T C C T

If you know one strand, you know both. That is why DNA can be copied.


Give students 30 seconds, then reveal. Optional extra: ask them to write their own 8-letter strand and swap with a neighbour, who writes the complementary strand. Advanced point if someone asks: the two strands run in opposite directions (antiparallel), labelled 5’ and 3’.

title: Understanding DNA
text:
The Double Helix


Focus on the SHAPE, not the chemistry. Start from the ladder: two sides (sugar–phosphate backbones) and rungs (base pairs). Then twist it. Points to make: (1) the backbone is on the outside and the bases, which carry the information, are on the inside, where they are protected; (2) every rung has the same width (purine + pyrimidine), so the helix is perfectly regular: 2 nm wide, one full turn every 10 base pairs (3.4 nm); (3) the two strands run in opposite directions, labelled 5′ and 3′ after the numbered carbons of the sugar (slide 8); (4) the strands are not exactly opposite each other, so the twist leaves a wide groove and a narrow groove (major and minor grooves). Proteins that read DNA, for example the ones that switch genes on and off, fit into the major groove and “feel” the bases without opening the helix. Who discovered this shape, and how? We will see it in the case study at the end of the lesson.

title: Understanding DNA
text:
Why 5’ and 3’?

 


The names come from the sugar (see slide 8). Its five carbon atoms are numbered 1′ to 5′. The prime sign (′) is there because the atoms of the base are also numbered (1, 2, 3…), so the sugar’s carbons get a prime to tell them apart. Read “5′” as “five prime”. In a strand, each phosphate is a bridge: it is attached to carbon 5′ of one sugar and carbon 3′ of the next sugar. So the strand has a direction, like an arrow: at one end there is a free phosphate on a 5′ carbon (the 5′ end), at the other end a free OH on a 3′ carbon (the 3′ end). Scientists always write DNA sequences from 5′ to 3′. Point at the pentagons: on the left strand they point up, on the right strand they are upside down, so the two strands are antiparallel. This is why base pairs fit neatly in the middle. Replication direction (bottom strip): DNA polymerase can only add a new nucleotide to the free OH on the 3′ end of the growing strand. The new nucleotide arrives with its phosphate on the 5′ side, and that phosphate bonds to the 3′ OH. So a new strand always grows 5′ → 3′, reading the template in the opposite direction (3′ → 5′). Because the two template strands are antiparallel, one new strand can be made continuously while the other is made in short pieces (Okazaki fragments) that are joined later: mention only if students ask, or link to the Amoeba Sisters video coming up. Ask: if one strand reads 5′-ATG-3′, how do you write its partner in the 5′ → 3′ direction? (5′-CAT-3′.)

title: Understanding DNA
text:
How Small Is DNA?

 


The helix is only 2 nm wide, but the DNA in one cell, unwound, is about 2 m long!


Use the scale: each step to the right is 1,000 times smaller. Milli = one thousandth, micro = one millionth, nano = one billionth (the same prefixes as in milligram, microsecond, nanotechnology). Ask: how many nanometres in a millimetre? (1,000,000.) 2 nm = 0.000002 mm: about 50,000 times thinner than a human hair. You cannot see a single DNA molecule with a light microscope. And yet each cell nucleus (about 6 µm across) holds about 2 m of DNA. How does it fit? Next slide. Next week, in the lab, you will extract DNA from fruit and see it with your own eyes: you will see millions of molecules clumped together, not a single one.

title: Understanding DNA
section: Estimate It: All the DNA in Your Body
text:
Estimate It: All the DNA in Your Body






Tip


A scientist’s estimate: about 2 m of DNA per cell × your number of cells = ?




Guess the number of cells in a human body
Multiply by 2 m
Compare with the distance from the Earth to the Sun: 150 million km


≈ 30 trillion cells × 2 m ≈ 60 billion km: enough to go to the Sun and back about 200 times.


This is a “Fermi estimate”: a rough calculation with round numbers, the way scientists check if an answer is reasonable. Let groups of students try it before revealing. Numbers: about 30 trillion (3 × 10^13) cells in a human body (Sender et al., 2016). 3 × 10^13 × 2 m = 6 × 10^13 m = 6 × 10^10 km. Sun and back = 3 × 10^8 km, so 6 × 10^10 / 3 × 10^8 = 200 trips. Critical-thinking twist (link to Session 2): this estimate has a hidden assumption! About 80% of our cells are red blood cells, and they have NO nucleus and no DNA. So the real answer is several times smaller, but still tens of round trips to the Sun. Popular websites quote very different numbers (“600 times to the Sun”, “17 times to Pluto”) because they make different assumptions. Ask: which assumptions would change the answer?

title: Understanding DNA
text:
Packing DNA: Chromosomes





DNA is wound around proteins called histones, like thread on a spool
It is then coiled again and again into chromosomes
Humans have 46 chromosomes (23 pairs): one set from each parent



The packaging is what lets 2 m of DNA fit into a nucleus a few micrometres wide. DNA + histones = chromatin. Before a cell divides, chromatin condenses into the X-shaped chromosomes you see in textbook pictures.

title: Understanding DNA
text:
Where Is DNA Found?





Mostly in the nucleus
A little in the mitochondria
In plants, also in the chloroplasts
Bacteria have no nucleus: their DNA floats in the cell



Mitochondria and chloroplasts have their own small DNA because they were once free-living bacteria swallowed by an ancestral cell (endosymbiosis). Mitochondrial DNA is inherited only from the mother, which is useful for tracing ancestry. We will meet this again in the forensic DNA session.

title: Understanding DNA
text:
DNA Replication: Copying the Code

The helix unzips → each strand is a template → new bases follow the pairing rule → two identical copies

Before every cell division, all 3 billion base pairs are copied. Each new molecule keeps one old strand and gets one new strand: this is called semi-conservative replication. The enzyme that unzips is helicase; the enzyme that adds new nucleotides is DNA polymerase. It makes about one mistake in a billion bases after proofreading. Those rare mistakes are mutations.

title: Understanding DNA
text:
DNA Replication: Video


Amoeba Sisters, “DNA Replication”. Play it, then ask: what does helicase do? What does DNA polymerase do? Why is the pairing rule essential for copying?

title: Understanding DNA
text:
What Is a Gene?

A gene is a stretch of DNA with the instructions to make one product, usually a protein.

Proteins do most of the work in a cell: enzymes, hormones like insulin, antibodies, the keratin in your hair. How the cell reads a gene to make a protein (DNA → RNA → protein) is the topic of Session 5, the “central dogma”. Every cell has the same DNA (same cookbook), but a liver cell and a brain cell read different recipes.

title: Understanding DNA
section: The Human Genome by Numbers — Guess First!
text:
The Human Genome by Numbers — Guess First!

Choose an answer for each question, then check.








Question
Answer




How many base pairs are in the human genome?
3 million · 3 billion · 3 trillion


How many protein-coding genes?
2,000 · 20,000 · 200,000


What fraction of the genome codes for proteins?
1.5 % · 15 % · 50 %


Typing it at 60 words per minute, 8 hours a day: how long?
6 months · 6 years · 60 years


How much of your DNA is unique to you?
0.1 % · 1 % · 10 %





Students guess on paper first (retrieval and prediction from Session 1!), then reveal answers one at a time. Typing: 3.1 billion letters; 60 words per minute ≈ 300 letters per minute; 8 h a day = 144,000 letters a day; 3.1 billion / 144,000 ≈ 21,500 days ≈ 59 years. The 1.5% refers to the parts of genes that are actually translated into protein (exons); whole genes, including introns, take up much more. The rest of the genome includes switches that turn genes on and off, and many repeated sequences. On the “0.1%”: two people differ at about 1 base in 1,000 (single-letter differences). Counting larger insertions and deletions too, the difference is somewhat bigger (around 0.5%), but 0.1% is the figure usually quoted.

title: Understanding DNA
section: Is the Human at the Top?
text:
Is the Human at the Top?







Fork fernthe biggest genome known



Bread wheat≈ 107,000 genes


Photos: Pol Fernández (CC BY 4.0); Patrick Alexander (CC0), via Wikimedia Commons




The photos: the fork fern Tmesipteris oblanceolata is a small plant, only 10–15 cm tall, that grows on tree trunks in New Caledonia, yet each of its cells holds about 100 m of DNA. Bread wheat (Triticum aestivum) is the wheat in our bread and pasta flour. Before showing the chart, ask: “Which organism do you think has the biggest genome? The most genes?” Most students will say humans. Then reveal. Genome size: the fork fern Tmesipteris oblanceolata (New Caledonia) holds the record, ≈ 160 billion base pairs, about 50 times ours (Fernández et al., 2024). Marbled lungfish ≈ 130 billion; axolotl ≈ 32 billion; bread wheat ≈ 16 billion (it has six copies of its genome, from three ancestral species). Gene counts: the fork fern has a “?” because its genome has only been weighed (measured by flow cytometry), never sequenced, so nobody knows how many genes it has. Bread wheat ≈ 107,000 (IWGSC, 2018), pea ≈ 45,000 (Kreplak et al., 2019), and the roundworm C. elegans, a 1 mm worm with about 1,000 cells, has about the same number of genes as us. This puzzle has a name: the “C-value paradox” (genome size does not match complexity). Why so much DNA? Large genomes are mostly filled with repeated sequences, and many plants have duplicated their whole genome during evolution. How do humans get complexity with only 20,000 genes? By controlling when and where genes are switched on, and by making several different proteins from one gene (alternative splicing, Session 5). Link to Session 2: the “hypothesis” that more genes means a more complex organism was tested by sequencing, and the data contradicted it. Numbers are rounded; different sources give slightly different values.

title: Understanding DNA
text:
Mutations: Changes to the Code

A mutation is a change in the DNA sequence. Its effect can be harmful, neutral or beneficial.

The cell reads DNA in three-letter “words” (codons), so the sentence analogy works well. A substitution changes one word; a deletion or insertion shifts the reading frame and garbles everything after it, so it is usually more harmful. Most mutations are neutral: they fall outside genes, or do not change the protein. Real example of “harmful AND beneficial”: the sickle-cell mutation (one letter, A → T) causes sickle-cell disease if you inherit two copies, but one copy protects against malaria. Mutations are the raw material of evolution: without them there would be no variation. Causes: copying errors during replication, UV light, some chemicals, radiation.

title: Understanding DNA
section: How Much DNA Do We Share?
text:
How Much DNA Do We Share?

With any other human: about 99.9 %
With a chimpanzee: about 99 %
With a mouse: about 85 % of the protein-coding DNA
With a fruit fly: about 60 % of our genes have a fly version







Warning


“You share 50 % of your DNA with a banana” is a popular claim. It really means many of our genes have a related version in plants. It does not mean half of your DNA letters are the same!




These similarities are strong evidence that all living things share common ancestors: the more distantly related, the less similar the DNA. Critical-thinking link to Session 2: always ask WHAT is being compared (whole genome? only genes? only protein-coding parts?) and HOW similarity is measured. Different methods give very different percentages for the same pair of species. Fruit flies are used in medical research because about 75% of human disease-related genes have a counterpart in the fly.

title: Understanding DNA
text:
Every Person Is Unique

0.1 % of 3 billion = 3 million differences between you and the person next to you.

0.1% sounds tiny, but 0.1% of 3 billion is 3 million letters. These differences contribute to eye colour, height, risk of some diseases, and so on. They are also what forensic DNA testing uses to identify people (Session 8). Except for identical twins, everyone’s DNA is unique.

title: Understanding DNA
text:
Background: What Was Known



1944: DNA is shown to carry genetic information
1950: Erwin Chargaff measures the four bases in many species
Nobody knows the shape of the molecule





Observation step of the scientific method. Ask students: what pattern do you see in the data? Answer: in every species, the amount of A is about equal to T, and G is about equal to C, but the A+T vs G+C ratio changes from species to species. These are “Chargaff’s rules”. Chargaff did not know WHY. Values are approximate (Chargaff’s data, rounded). The 1944 experiments were by Avery, MacLeod and McCarty.

title: Understanding DNA
text:
The Data: Photo 51





May 1952, King’s College London
Rosalind Franklin and her student Raymond Gosling shoot X-rays through DNA fibres
The X-shaped pattern means a helix; the spacing gives its size



Data collection step. Franklin was an expert in X-ray crystallography: X-rays are scattered by the molecule and the pattern on film reveals its structure. Photo 51 needed about 100 hours of exposure. From her images and measurements Franklin worked out that the backbone is on the outside and that the molecule has a regular repeating structure. Precision link to Session 2: her measurements were careful and repeated.

title: Understanding DNA
text:
Reading Photo 51


Data analysis step of the scientific method: how do you get a 3D shape from a 2D photo? X-rays bounce off the regularly repeating parts of the molecule and make a pattern of dark spots on the film. Reveal the clues one at a time and let students guess what each means. (1) The X: a zigzag seen from the side gives an X-shaped pattern, and a helix seen from the side looks like a zigzag, so the X means a helix. The steeper the X, the flatter the coils. (2) The stripes (layer lines) along the arms of the X: their spacing tells you how long one full turn is, 3.4 nm. Counter-intuitive but important: the CLOSER the stripes on the film, the LONGER the repeat in the molecule (diffraction works “upside down”, like the reciprocal). (3) The 4th stripe is missing: with a single helix it would be there. It disappears because there are two strands, shifted by about 3/8 of a turn, so their signals cancel at that position. Two strands that are not opposite each other means a major and a minor groove (slide 13). (4) The strong arcs at the very top and bottom: something repeats every 0.34 nm along the molecule: the flat base pairs stacked like a pile of coins. 3.4 nm ÷ 0.34 nm = 10 base pairs per turn. The width (about 2 nm) comes from the spacing of the spots across the pattern. Franklin also showed, from how DNA takes up water, that the phosphate backbone must be on the outside. Watson recalled that when he saw Photo 51 “my mouth fell open and my pulse began to race”: the X told him immediately it was a helix.

title: Understanding DNA
section: From Photo 51 to the Double Helix
text:
From Photo 51 to the Double Helix




Photo 51: the X-ray pattern of DNA
Find the X
Turn each arm 90°: the slopes of a zigzag
A helix seen from the side looks like a zigzag
Missing 4th stripe → a second strand, shifted
Arcs top and bottom → 10 base pairs per turn


⏸ Pause
Step ▸
↺ Restart





An animation of the reasoning on the previous slide. It starts by itself when the slide appears; use “Step ▸” to stop after each stage and ask the class what comes next, or “Pause”/“Restart”. Stages: (1) Photo 51. (2) The X. (3) Physics of diffraction: each arm of the X is at right angles to a repeating slope in the molecule, so turning each arm by 90° gives the two slopes of a zigzag. (4) A helix seen from the side IS a zigzag (smoothed into a wave): watch it start to turn in 3D. (5) The missing 4th stripe means a second strand, shifted about 3/8 of a turn, which creates the major and minor grooves. (6) The arcs at the top and bottom of the photo give the 0.34 nm spacing of the stacked base pairs: 10 per turn of 3.4 nm; the width is 2 nm. This is a simplified explanation for students: real X-ray diffraction analysis is mathematical, but the logic is the same.

title: Understanding DNA
text:
The Hypothesis: Building Models




In Cambridge, James Watson and Francis Crick build models of metal and cardboard.
Their first model (1951) was wrong: bases on the outside, three strands.


Hypothesis step. Watson and Crick did not do experiments themselves: they combined other people’s data into a model, and tested whether the model fitted ALL the data. Their first model was rejected after Franklin pointed out that it contradicted her measurements. Science is a cycle: back to the drawing board! In January 1953, Maurice Wilkins (Franklin’s colleague) showed Photo 51 to Watson without Franklin’s knowledge, and Watson and Crick also saw a report with her data. This is an important ethics discussion point for the end of the case study.

title: Understanding DNA
section: “We Have Found the Secret of Life”
text:
“We Have Found the Secret of Life”





28 February 1953: the new model fits Photo 51 and Chargaff’s rules
Crick announces it at lunch in the Eagle pub, Cambridge
April 1953: published in Nature, a paper of just one page



The key insight was base pairing: A with T and G with C. That explained Chargaff’s rules immediately (A = T, G = C). It also gave the same width for every rung, matching Franklin’s data. Communication step: in the same issue of Nature there were also papers by Franklin & Gosling and by Wilkins with the X-ray evidence. The pub still has a blue plaque about the discovery.

title: Understanding DNA
text:
Testing the Prediction

“It has not escaped our notice that the specific pairing we have postulated immediately suggests a possible copying mechanism for the genetic material.”
— Watson & Crick, 1953


Prediction: each new DNA molecule keeps one old strand and gets one new strand
1958: Meselson and Stahl test it with bacteria — the prediction is confirmed


A good hypothesis makes predictions that could turn out false (falsifiability, Session 2). The double-helix model predicted semi-conservative replication: exactly what we drew earlier in the lesson. Meselson and Stahl grew bacteria with “heavy” nitrogen, then switched to “light” nitrogen, and measured the weight of the DNA after each generation. The results matched the prediction perfectly. The model survived a real test, so it got much stronger. Ask: what result would have proved the model wrong?

title: Understanding DNA
text:
Rosalind Franklin: Video


TED-Ed, “Rosalind Franklin: DNA’s unsung hero”. Play it, then move to the discussion on the next slide.

title: Understanding DNA
text:
Conclusion & Impact

1962: Nobel Prize to Watson, Crick and Wilkins
Franklin had died in 1958, aged 37: the Nobel is never given after death
The double helix opened the way to modern genetics and biotechnology







Note


Discussion: Was it fair to use Franklin’s data without asking her? What does it teach us about credit in science?




Let students discuss in pairs for 2–3 minutes, then share. Points to bring out: science is collaborative, and data from many people (Chargaff, Franklin, Gosling, Wilkins) led to the model. Correct credit and permission to use data are part of research ethics. Peer review and publication (Session 2) are also about giving credit. Franklin went on to do important work on the structure of viruses.

title: Understanding DNA
section: From One Molecule to the Whole Genome
text:
From One Molecule to the Whole Genome


Human Genome Project (1990–2003): the first reading of all ~3 billion letters
2022: the last gaps were finally filled in
Today genome sequencing is used in medicine, ancestry, agriculture and forensics


Fifty years after the double helix, the whole human genome was read. The 2003 version still had gaps (about 8% was missing, mostly highly repetitive regions); the Telomere-to-Telomere (T2T) consortium published the first complete, gap-free sequence in 2022. The cost fell faster than computer prices: from billions of dollars to a few hundred. We will look at how sequencing works in the Biotech and Bioinformatics sessions.

title: Understanding DNA
text:
Recap

DNA is a polymer of nucleotides: phosphate + sugar + base (A, T, G, C)
Base pairing (A–T, G–C) makes the two strands complementary
DNA is a double helix, packed into chromosomes, mostly in the nucleus
Replication copies DNA: each strand is a template
A gene is a stretch of DNA that codes for a product, usually a protein
Mutations change the sequence: harmful, neutral or beneficial
The double helix was found by combining data (Chargaff, Franklin) and models (Watson & Crick)

title: Understanding DNA
text:
Classroom Exercise: Exploring DNA








Worksheet handed out on paper in class. It covers:

True or False: correct 5 statements about DNA
Matching: match 8 terms (nucleotide, gene, genome, chromosome…) to their definitions
Complementary strands: write the missing strand and use Chargaff’s rules
The double helix story: link each event to a step of the scientific method



Hand out the paper worksheet (material/dna-worksheet.pdf) and give students time to work individually or in pairs. Walk around and help, then go through the answers together before the end of class. Answer key. Part A: 1 False, the double helix was described in 1953; 2 True; 3 False, A pairs with T, G with C; 4 False, most mutations are neutral; 5 False, humans have 46 chromosomes (23 pairs). Part B: 1-d, 2-f, 3-a, 4-h, 5-b, 6-g, 7-c, 8-e. Part C: (1) AATCGGTACG; (2) GCTTAAGCAT; (3) T = 30%, G = 20%, C = 20%; (4) G–C-rich DNA, because each G–C pair has 3 hydrogen bonds instead of 2. Part D: a = observation, b = data collection, c = hypothesis, d = revising the hypothesis, e = communicating the conclusion, f = testing a prediction.

title: Understanding DNA
text:
Overview
DNA (deoxyribonucleic acid) is the molecule that stores the instructions for every living thing. It is a long chain of nucleotides, and its four bases (A, T, G, C) pair up in a fixed way: A with T, G with C. That simple rule explains the double helix shape, how DNA is copied before a cell divides, and how a change in a single letter (a mutation) can make a difference.

title: Understanding DNA
text:
Key Vocabulary


nucleotide — the building block of DNA: a phosphate group, a sugar (deoxyribose) and a base
base pair — two bases joined by hydrogen bonds: A–T or G–C
complementary — matching according to the pairing rule; each DNA strand is complementary to the other
double helix — the shape of DNA: two strands twisted like a spiral ladder
chromosome — a tightly packed structure of DNA wound around proteins (histones); humans have 46
replication — the copying of DNA before a cell divides; each strand is a template for a new one
gene — a stretch of DNA with the instructions for one product, usually a protein
genome — the complete set of DNA of an organism (about 3 billion base pairs in humans)
mutation — a change in the DNA sequence; it can be harmful, neutral or beneficial

Case Study: The Double Helix
The discovery of DNA’s structure in 1953 is a real example of the scientific method. Erwin Chargaff’s data showed that A ≈ T and G ≈ C, and Rosalind Franklin’s X-ray image (Photo 51) showed a helix. James Watson and Francis Crick combined these data into a model, which predicted how DNA is copied, and that prediction was confirmed in 1958. title: How to Study
text:
Key Vocabulary

Retrieval practice — bringing information to mind from memory (closing the book and writing or sketching what you know), rather than re-reading it.


Spaced practice — spreading study over time, with gaps between sessions, instead of cramming.


Dual coding — combining words and visuals (diagrams, timelines, drawings) to represent the same information.


Interleaving — switching between different topics or types of problems during a study session, instead of studying one topic until it is finished.


Concrete examples — specific cases that illustrate an abstract idea.


Elaboration — explaining an idea in detail, asking how and why it works, and connecting it to what you already know.


Multitasking — the myth of doing several tasks at once. In practice we switch rapidly between tasks, and attention can only be on one task at a time.


Pomodoro technique — studying in focused blocks (about 25 minutes) separated by short breaks.

What is this course?
Scientific English is a science course taught entirely in English. We look at real biology (the scientific method, DNA, biotechnology, bioinformatics, evolution and plants) and, at the same time, we learn the English that scientists use to describe it.
You do not need perfect English to take part. Mistakes are part of learning a language, just as failed experiments are part of science. What matters is that you try to speak, read and write in English every lesson.

title: Understanding the Scientific Method
text:
What is the Scientific Method?



A way to investigate the world and answer questions using observation and experiment
A step-by-step process for exploring how things work and why
Think of it as a detective’s toolkit for solving mysteries about the world





This slide sets the tone. The scientific method is not just a boring recipe — it’s a practical problem-solving tool that they use every day, even if they don’t call it that. The detective analogy works well because it emphasizes curiosity and investigation.

title: Understanding the Scientific Method
text:
Curiosity Drives Discovery
Science starts with asking questions about the world around us:


Ask students for their own “why” questions about the world before moving on. Any of them could start a scientific investigation.

title: Understanding the Scientific Method
text:
The Seven Steps


The seven steps: 1. Observation, 2. Question, 3. Hypothesis, 4. Experiment, 5. Data collection, 6. Data analysis, 7. Conclusion. Emphasize that this is a cycle, not a straight line — scientists often go back and revise.

title: Understanding the Scientific Method
text:
An Everyday Example: The Toaster









This toaster sequence walks through steps 1–4 concretely: observation (toaster won’t toast), question (why?), hypothesis (maybe the outlet), and prediction (if we try a different outlet it will work). Use this to show that the scientific method isn’t just for labs — students do this at home.

title: Understanding the Scientific Method
text:
Testing the Prediction

If the toaster still doesn’t work in the new outlet, the hypothesis is rejected — time to try another one (maybe it’s the toaster itself, not the outlet).

If the prediction fails, we don’t give up — we form a new hypothesis and test again. This is why the scientific method is a cycle. Ask students: what other hypotheses could explain the toaster not working?

title: Understanding the Scientific Method
section: Science is a Cycle, Not a Line
text:
Science is a Cycle, Not a Line



We often go back, revise our ideas, and try again
Findings are shared so others can learn and build on them
The scientific method isn’t only for labs — we use it every day

title: Understanding the Scientific Method
text:
Step 1 — Observation
Careful, systematic scrutiny of the world.
Sources of observations:


Sources of observations: direct sensory experience (what you see, hear, measure yourself), literature review (books and scientific articles), and findings from previous studies.

title: Understanding the Scientific Method
text:
Step 2 — Question
A clear, focused inquiry based on the observation.

Vocabulary: ambiguous — unclear or open to more than one interpretation.



Vague questions lead to vague hypotheses, and those lead to experiments that are hard to design. “Do plants like light?” cannot be tested directly: what does “like” mean? The focused version says what we change (amount of light), on what (bean plants), what we measure (height) and when (2 weeks). Ask students to make another vague question focused.

title: Understanding the Scientific Method
text:
Step 3 — Hypothesis


A testable and falsifiable statement proposing an answer to the question.

Expresses a cause-and-effect relationship
Falsifiability: it must be possible to prove it wrong

Example: If I plug the toaster into another outlet, then it will work.




A useful pattern for students: “If … then …”. Researchers may also compare several alternative hypotheses for the same question (for the toaster: the outlet, the fuse, the toaster itself).

title: Understanding the Scientific Method
text:
Correlation Is Not Causation







Warning


Watch out for spurious correlations — two things changing together doesn’t mean one causes the other. https://www.tylervigen.com/spurious-correlations




Ice cream sales and shark attacks rise and fall together, but ice cream does not cause shark attacks. A third factor, hot weather, causes both: more people buy ice cream and more people swim in the sea. Ask: what is the hidden cause? Then open the Tyler Vigen site for funny real examples.

title: Understanding the Scientific Method
text:
The Null Hypothesis

Null hypothesis (H₀) — the claim of no effect: any change we observe is just due to chance.


H₁: Studying with flashcards improves exam scores
H₀: Studying with flashcards has no effect on exam scores
An experiment gathers evidence to reject H₀ — it doesn’t prove H₁







Important


A scientist’s job is not to prove they are right. You design the experiment to try to prove your own hypothesis wrong — if it survives that attempt, it gets stronger.




This is a subtle but important idea: scientists don’t set out to prove their hypothesis directly. They test whether the data make the “nothing is happening” explanation (H₀) unlikely. If exam scores are clearly higher with flashcards, we reject H₀ in favour of H₁. If scores are about the same, we fail to reject H₀ — that doesn’t mean H₀ is true, only that we don’t have enough evidence against it. This connects back to falsifiability: H₀ is the default, skeptical position you need evidence to overturn. Philosophy of science point (Popper): good science is not about confirming what you already believe — hunting only for evidence that agrees with you is confirmation bias. A real test is one that COULD have proven you wrong and didn’t. Ask students: what would the null hypothesis be for the toaster example, or for Fleming’s penicillin observation? And how could Fleming have been wrong?

title: Understanding the Scientific Method
text:
Step 4 — Experiment
Planning and organizing the procedure that will test the hypothesis.

Independent variable — the one we deliberately change
Dependent variable — the one we measure

title: Understanding the Scientific Method
text:
Identifying Variables — Try It



Scenario
Independent variable
Dependent variable




Plant growth
Amount of sunlight
Height of plants


Drug dosage
Dosage of a drug
Heart rate


Exam scores
?
Exam scores




What could the independent variable be in the exam scores example? (hours studied? sleep? something else?)


Pause here and get answers from students. Common ones: hours studied, amount of sleep, caffeine intake, test anxiety. This is where you can tie back to their real lives — they’re all doing experiments (studying vs not studying, sleeping vs staying up) and observing the outcome (exam score). Ask: which variable would YOU want to test?

title: Understanding the Scientific Method
section: Step 5 — Data Collection: Two Types of Data
text:
Step 5 — Data Collection: Two Types of Data









Qualitative
Quantitative




Nature
Descriptive, not easily measured
Numerical, measurable


Example
Colour of a flower, texture
Height (cm), temperature (°C)





Form: qualitative data are observations and categories; quantitative data are numbers from measurements or counts. Analysis: qualitative data are analysed by themes and content; quantitative data with statistical methods. Both types are valuable. Qualitative data captures nuance and description — “the plant looks healthier, has more vibrant green.” Quantitative data is precise and analyzable — “the plant is 25.3 cm tall.” In Fleming’s penicillin experiment, qualitative observation (the clear zone around the mould) led him to the discovery, but quantitative data (how much bacterial growth was inhibited, concentration of the substance needed) was crucial for developing it as a medicine.

title: Understanding the Scientific Method
text:
Precision vs. Accuracy










Precision
Accuracy




Definition
How closely repeated measurements agree with each other
How close a measurement is to the true value


Associated with
Consistency, reliability
Correctness, no systematic error


Example
Weighing something 5× and always getting 12.3 g
Weighing something and getting the true 12.5 g









Tip


It’s possible to be precise but not accurate — consistent measurements can still all be wrong if there’s a systematic error.

title: Understanding the Scientific Method
text:
Precision vs. Accuracy — Try It

For each target: is it precise? Is it accurate?

Show the unlabeled targets and ask students to call out, for each quadrant, whether it shows high/low precision and high/low accuracy, before revealing the labeled version on the next slide.

title: Understanding the Scientific Method
text:
Precision vs. Accuracy — Visualized


Walk through each quadrant. Top-left (scattered, off-center): neither precise nor accurate — measurements are all over the place and far from the bullseye. Top-right (clustered, off-center): precise but NOT accurate — they’re consistent with each other, but they’re clustered in the wrong place. Bottom-left (scattered, centered): accurate but not precise — they’re scattered, but on average they hit the target. Bottom-right (clustered, centered): both precise AND accurate — the gold standard. Real-world example: a broken scale that always reads 2 kg too high is precise (consistent) but not accurate (wrong value).

title: Understanding the Scientific Method
text:
The Control Group


Baseline comparison (no treatment) — keep everything else constant


Vocabulary: confounding variable — an outside factor that could distort the result.


Purpose of a control group: a baseline comparison (the normal state, without treatment); minimizing confounding variables by keeping everything else constant; establishing cause and effect; a standard for comparison against the experimental group. Without a control group, you can’t tell if the outcome was caused by your variable or something else. Example: testing a new study technique on one class but not another. But if the class getting the technique is also more motivated, how do you know which caused the better grades? A control group that differs ONLY in the treatment lets you isolate the effect. This is the most common reason experiments fail — they don’t properly control confounding variables.

title: Understanding the Scientific Method
text:
Randomization & Replication



Randomization helps eliminate bias: assign subjects to groups by chance (e.g. a coin flip), not by choice — otherwise, say, the most motivated students could all end up in the same group
Replication (repeating the trial) helps ensure results are reliable





The image shows the same treatment (star, square, circle shapes) randomly assigned to different groups across multiple repetitions. Randomization prevents you from accidentally biasing which subjects get which treatment — maybe without randomization, the most motivated students would all end up in the experimental group by chance. Replication (repeating the experiment 4 times here) shows that results are not a fluke. If you get similar results every time, you’re confident in your finding.

title: Understanding the Scientific Method
text:
Step 6 — Data Analysis

Organizing data (data cleaning): tables, graphs, charts
Descriptive statistics: mean, median, standard deviation
Graphical representations: scatter plots, bar graphs, histograms, line graphs

title: Understanding the Scientific Method
text:
Step 7 — Conclusion



Compare results with the hypothesis: supported, or contradicted?
Assess validity and look for alternative explanations
Communicate findings — papers undergo peer review before publication





Validity means: reliability of the data, rigor of the design, possible confounders. Scientists also consider statistical significance (could the result be due to chance?), generalizability (does it apply to other cases?) and the broader implications. A good conclusion doesn’t just say “we were right” or “we were wrong.” It evaluates HOW CONFIDENT we should be in the result. Did we test enough subjects? Enough times? Could something else have caused the outcome? What’s next? For Fleming, the conclusion was: this substance looks promising for medical use — but more research (which took 12 years and multiple scientists) was needed to develop it into a usable drug. This is why peer review matters: other experts check your logic and methods before your work becomes trusted.

title: Understanding the Scientific Method
text:
Observation


In September 1928, Alexander Fleming was studying Staphylococcus bacteria at St. Mary’s Hospital, London.
He left petri dishes on his workbench while on vacation.

title: Understanding the Scientific Method
text:
Observation (continued)


Upon returning, he noticed one dish had mould growing on it — with a clear area around the mould where bacteria seemed to be killed.




This is the key observation — most scientists would have cursed and thrown away contaminated plates. But Fleming was curious enough to wonder WHY the bacteria died. This is the foundation of every great scientific discovery: curiosity about an unexpected result. Without that curiosity, penicillin would still be sitting in dirty lab dishes unnoticed.

title: Understanding the Scientific Method
text:
Question & Hypothesis


Question: What killed the bacteria near the mould?
Hypothesis: The mould (later identified as Penicillium) releases a substance that inhibits bacterial growth.

title: Understanding the Scientific Method
text:
Experiment
Fleming:

Isolated the mould
Extracted its secretions
Tested the secretions against various bacteria, including Staphylococcus

title: Understanding the Scientific Method
text:
Data & Analysis


The substance killed a wide range of bacteria — but was not toxic to human cells.
This substance was later named penicillin.




Fleming’s original 1929 figure, British Journal of Experimental Pathology




Show them the actual historical 1929 publication photo. This is real data from a real experiment over 90 years ago. The key finding: the mould secretion killed bacteria in a test tube without harming human tissue. This was the data that mattered — not just that bacteria died, but that it could be used safely. The three labels in the photo show: the Penicillium colony (the source), the zone where Staphylococcus is undergoing lysis (dying), and normal Staphylococcus colony far away. This figure was published in the British Journal of Experimental Pathology — Fleming communicated his findings to the scientific community.

title: Understanding the Scientific Method
text:
Conclusion & Impact



Penicillin was recognized as a potential antibiotic
In the 1940s, Howard Florey and Ernst Boris Chain scaled up production
This marked the beginning of the antibiotic era in medicine
1945: Fleming, Florey and Chain shared the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine




Lives saved to date: over 200 million

title: Understanding the Scientific Method
text:
Recap

Science moves through observation → question → hypothesis → experiment → data → analysis → conclusion — as a cycle
A good hypothesis is testable and falsifiable
Distinguish precision from accuracy
Control groups, randomization and replication make experiments trustworthy
Fleming’s discovery of penicillin is a real-world example of this whole process

title: Understanding the Scientific Method
section: Classroom Exercise: Exploring the Scientific Method
text:
Classroom Exercise: Exploring the Scientific Method








Worksheet handed out on paper in class. It covers:

True or False — correct 5 statements about the scientific method
Matching — match 8 terms (hypothesis, control group, independent/dependent variable…) to their definitions
Identifying — read 3 real scenarios and identify the independent variable, dependent variable, experimental group and control group in each



Hand out the paper worksheet now and give students time to work through it individually or in pairs. This is a good formative check: the True/False section tests vocabulary, Matching tests definitions, and the three scenarios (dog food, sunscreen, plant growth) test whether students can actually identify variables and groups in a new context, not just recite definitions. Walk around and help, then go through the answers together before the end of class.
